scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Emerging in 2010s Paris, Urban Kiz detached from Kizomba's grounded hips by straightening the legs, tracking geometric lines, and pausing weight transfers through a delayed 'and-principle.'
This is Urban Kiz. 2010s.

Title card: Urban Kiz · France · 2010s

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Urban Kiz developed in Paris during the 2010s as a divergence from Kizomba.
During the 2000s, Kizomba was exported abroad and introduced by the Angolan diaspora into countries such as Portugal, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Spain.
Early video distribution on YouTube and Vimeo helped popularize alternative approaches.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Urban Kiz functions as a modern social partner dance.

Its development and naming reflected an intentional effort to carve out a distinct identity for dancers blending street dance dynamics with partnered connection, separating it from traditional Angolan Kizomba while maintaining historical lineage.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Urban Kiz is a partner dance characterized by straight legs, upright frames, and higher muscular tension and movement energy compared to grounded Kizomba.
Dancers move along straight lines, executing sudden reversals or turning at perpendicular angles.
Choreographic mechanics frequently employ hip-hop elements such as stops, taps, and isolations, alongside tango-derived pivots and follower pirouettes.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha (Tarraxa), Afrobeat, and remixes featuring R&B, Rap, Dance, and Hip Hop.
The music features dynamic shifts in pace, containing bridge transitions to slower tempos, abrupt breaks, and accelerations that dancers match through syncopations and isolations.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key pioneers include Curtis Seldon and Cherazad (Sherazad) Benyoucef, who reshaped the movement around 2013, as well as dancers Enah Lebon and Moun.
The dance originated in Paris, France, and while it remains most prevalent in Europe, by 2020 it spread across dozens of annual festivals across all six developed continents.

Urban Kiz directly diverged from Angolan Kizomba, while integrating technical figures and movement concepts from Argentine Tango (such as pivots) as well as body isolations, stops, and taps from Hip Hop.
